data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The distinction between genuine reliability and checklist coincidence is itself undecidable without a process-tracing signal: outcome data alone cannot separate them because they produce identical outcomes. A single evaluation can distinguish them only if it includes process observations (e.g., response times, intermediate judgments, verbal protocols) that reveal whether the panel is reasoning through the checklist or merely pattern-matching it.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If process traces are not collected or are too noisy to interpret, the distinction remains inaccessible even with outcome data.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If panelists can fake process traces (e.g., generate plausible explanations post hoc), the signal is contaminated.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the checklist is so simple that both genuine and coincidental followers produce identical process traces, the distinction is unobservable.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Genuine reliability means the checklist supports a reasoning process: the panelist understands why each step matters and can adapt when steps fail. Coincidence means the checklist is applied as a lookup table: steps are followed without comprehension. These differ in process, not outcome. A single evaluation with only outcome data observes identical performance. But if the evaluation includes process traces\u2014response time, intermediate step judgments, or explanation quality\u2014then genuine and coincidental compliance diverge: genuine reasoners slow down and adjust on ambiguous items; coincidental followers do not.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
